{{Short description|Removal of square roots from denominators}}
In [[elementary algebra]], '''root rationalisation''' (or '''rationalization''') is a process by which [[nth root|radical]]s in the [[denominator]] of an [[Fraction (mathematics)#Algebraic fractions|algebraic fraction]] are eliminated.

If the denominator is a [[monomial]] in some radical, say <math>a{\sqrt[n]{x}}^k,</math> with {{math|''k'' < ''n''}}, rationalisation consists of multiplying the numerator and the denominator by <math>\sqrt[n]{x}^{n - k}</math>, and replacing <math>{\sqrt[n]{x}}^n</math> by {{mvar|x}} (this is allowed, as, by definition, a [[nth root|{{mvar|n}}th root]] of {{mvar|x}} is a number that has {{mvar|x}} as its {{mvar|n}}th power).  If  {{math|''k'' ≥ ''n''}}, one writes {{math|1=''k'' = ''qn'' + ''r''}} with {{math|0 ≤ ''r'' < ''n''}} ([[Euclidean division]]), and <math>{\sqrt[n]{x}}^k = x^q\sqrt[n]x^r;</math> then one proceeds as above by multiplying by <math>\sqrt[n]{x}^{n - r}.</math>

If the denominator is [[linear function|linear]] in some square root, say <math>a+b\sqrt{x},</math> rationalisation consists of multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the [[Conjugate (square roots)|conjugate]] <math>a-b\sqrt{x},</math> and expanding the product in the denominator.

This technique may be extended to any algebraic denominator, by multiplying the numerator and the denominator by all [[algebraic conjugate]]s of the denominator, and expanding the new denominator into the [[field norm|norm]] of the old denominator. However, except in special cases, the resulting fractions may have huge numerators and denominators, and, therefore, the technique is generally used only in the above elementary cases.

== Rationalisation of a monomial square root and cube root ==

For the fundamental technique, the numerator and denominator must be multiplied by the same factor.

Example 1:

: <math>\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}}</math>

To rationalise this kind of [[expression (mathematics)|expression]], bring in the factor <math>\sqrt{5}</math>:

: <math>\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{{10\sqrt{5}}}{\left(\sqrt{5}\right)^2}</math>

The [[square root]] disappears from the denominator, because <math>\left(\sqrt 5\right)^2= 5</math> by definition of a square root:

: <math>\frac{{10\sqrt{5}}}{\left(\sqrt{5}\right)^2} = \frac{10\sqrt{5}}{5} = 2\sqrt{5},</math>
which is the result of the rationalisation.

Example 2:

: <math>\frac{10}{\sqrt[3]{a}}</math>

To rationalise this radical, bring in the factor <math>\sqrt[3]{a}^2</math>:

: <math>\frac{10}{\sqrt[3]{a}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt[3]{a}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt[3]{a}^2}{\sqrt[3]{a}^2} = \frac{{10\sqrt[3]{a}^2}}{\sqrt[3]{a}^3}</math>

The cube root disappears from the denominator, because it is cubed; so

:  <math>\frac{{10\sqrt[3]{a}^2}}{\sqrt[3]{a}^3} = \frac{10\sqrt[3]{a}^2}{a},</math>

which is the result of the rationalisation.

== Dealing with more square roots ==

For a [[denominator]] that is:

:<math>\sqrt{2}\pm \sqrt{3}\,</math>

Rationalisation can be achieved by multiplying by the [[Conjugate (square roots)|conjugate]]:

:<math>\sqrt{2} \mp \sqrt{3}\,</math>

and applying the [[difference of two squares]] identity, which here will yield &minus;1. To get this result, the entire fraction should be multiplied by

:<math>\frac{ \sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3} }{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{3}} = 1.</math>

This technique works much more generally. It can easily be adapted to remove one square root at a time, i.e. to rationalise

:<math>x \pm \sqrt{y}\,</math>

by multiplication by

:<math>x \mp \sqrt{y}</math>

Example:

:<math>\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}\pm \sqrt{5}}</math>

The fraction must be multiplied by a quotient containing <math>{\sqrt{3}\mp \sqrt{5}}</math>.

:<math>\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5}} = \frac{3(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5})}{\sqrt{3}^2 - \sqrt{5}^2}</math>

Now, we can proceed to remove the square roots in the denominator:

: <math>\frac{{3(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5}) }}{\sqrt{3}^2 - \sqrt{5}^2} = \frac{ 3 (\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{5} ) }{ 3 - 5 } = \frac{ 3( \sqrt{3}-\sqrt{5} )  }{-2}</math>

Example 2:

This process also works with [[complex numbers]] with <math>i=\sqrt{-1}</math>

:<math>\frac{7}{1\pm \sqrt{-5}}</math>

The fraction must be multiplied by a quotient containing <math>{1\mp \sqrt{-5}}</math>.

:<math>\frac{7}{1+\sqrt{-5}} \cdot \frac{1-\sqrt{-5}}{1-\sqrt{-5}} = \frac{7(1-\sqrt{-5})}{1^2 - \sqrt{-5}^2} = \frac{ 7 (1 - \sqrt{-5} ) }{ 1 - (-5) } = \frac{ 7 -7\sqrt{5} i }{6}</math>

==Generalizations==

Rationalisation can be extended to all [[algebraic number]]s and [[algebraic function]]s (as an application of [[norm form]]s). For example, to rationalise a [[cube root]], two linear factors involving [[cube roots of unity]] should be used, or equivalently a quadratic factor.

==References==
This material is carried in classic algebra texts. For example:

*[[George Chrystal]], ''Introduction to Algebra: For the Use of Secondary Schools and Technical Colleges'' is a nineteenth-century text, first edition 1889, in print ({{isbn|1402159072}}); a trinomial example with square roots is on p.&nbsp;256, while a general theory of rationalising factors for surds is on pp.&nbsp;189&ndash;199.
